questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=8-{x}^{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u={x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=8-{x}^{3}$ is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & -1 & -\infty  \\ u & 9 & \infty \end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{8-{x}^{3}}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{\infty }^{9}(-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{u}})\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{9}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{8-{x}^{3}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{9}^{a}\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[2\sqrt{u}]}_{9}^{a} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{9}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot \infty  \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the integral is divergent.

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{2z+1}}\,\text{d}z & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{2z+1}}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{3}{2}(2z+1)^{2/3}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[(2z+1)^{2/3}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }((2a+1)^{2/3}-1) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \infty  \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the integral is divergent.

questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u={x}^{3}+1.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{3}+1$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{({x}^{3}+1)^{5}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{5}}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{5}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{u}^{-5/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{u}^{-5/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{-3/2}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{a}^{3}}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Upper Limit Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=x+1.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x+1$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{(x+1)^{5}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{3}{{u}^{5}}\,\text{d}u
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{(x+1)^{5}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{3}{{u}^{5}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }3{u}^{-5}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}3{u}^{-5}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{3}{4}{u}^{-4}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{u}^{-4}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\frac{1}{{a}^{4}}-\frac{1}{{1}^{4}}] \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Lower Limit
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=5\theta -1.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}\theta }=5\,⟹\,\text{d}u=5\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $\theta \to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=5\theta -1$ is as follows:

| $\theta $ | $-\infty $ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\infty $ | $-1$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{12}{(5\theta -1)^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta ={\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{12}{5{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{12}{5{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{12}{5}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}{u}^{-2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{12}{5}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-{u}^{-1}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{12}{5}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{u}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{12}{5}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\frac{1}{(-1)}-\frac{1}{a}] \\  & =-\frac{12}{5}\cdot (-1-0) \\  & =\frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
